## Collaboration Question 4

## Load in data

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(ggpubr)

# Load the cleaned PRS data
load("data/prs_processed.Rda")

# Check the structure of the cleaned PRS dataset
glimpse(prs_data)

# View the first few rows
head(prs_data)

# Load in gait data
load("data/gait.Rda")

# Convert this table into a tidy "long" data frame:
clean_gait_data <- gait_data %>% pivot_longer(cols = 5:last_col(),
                           names_to = "Time_of_measurement_seconds",
                           values_to = "Degrees_off_vertical_orientation" )

# Then convert values in the column "Times of measurement" into numeric time.
clean_gait_data <- clean_gait_data %>% mutate(Time_of_measurement_seconds = sub("_.*", "", Time_of_measurement_seconds))

# Calculate descriptive statistics
summary_data <- clean_gait_data %>% 
group_by(donorid, treatment, exercise,age) %>% 
  # Because the measure have negative values, all values are converted to positive before calculating the mean
  summarise(avg_imbalance = mean(sqrt(Degrees_off_vertical_orientation^2)),
            median_imbalance = median(sqrt(Degrees_off_vertical_orientation^2)),
            sd_imbalance = sd(Degrees_off_vertical_orientation)
            ) 
# Run this to see descriptive stats for each patient
summary_data

```

## Merge both datasets

```{r}
# Merge PRS and gait data together
prs_gait <- prs_data %>%
  inner_join(summary_data, by = "donorid")

# Check the merged dataset
glimpse(prs_gait)

# Check number of matched participants
nrow(prs_gait)
```

## Visualise the relationship

Plot relationship between PRS and gait, then take into account age and exercise status.

```{r prs-gait-scatterplot}
# Visualise the relationship between PRS and gait imbalance
prs_gait |> 
  ggplot(aes(
    x = PRS,
    y = avg_imbalance
  )) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  labs(
    title = "Relationship between PRS and gait imbalance",
    x = "Polygenic Risk Score (PRS)",
    y = "Gait"
  ) +
  theme_classic()

# Introduce patient covariants: drug
prs_gait %>% 
  ggplot(aes(PRS, avg_imbalance, colour = treatment)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  labs(
    title = "Relationship between PRS and gait imbalance",
    x = "Polygenic Risk Score (PRS)",
    y = "Gait"
  ) +
  theme_classic()

# Introduce patient covariants: exercise
prs_gait %>% 
  ggplot(aes(PRS, avg_imbalance, colour = exercise)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  labs(
    title = "Relationship between PRS and gait imbalance",
    x = "Polygenic Risk Score (PRS)",
    y = "Gait"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

## Analysis of correlation between gait and PRS and how drug treatment and exercise status affects this relationship

### Normality check of Gait and PRS

```{r prs-normality}
# Check normality of PRS
ggplot(prs_gait,aes(sample = PRS))+
  geom_qq() +
  geom_qq_line()

shapiro.test(prs_gait$PRS)


```

```{r gait-normality}
# Check normality of gait imbalance
ggplot(prs_gait,aes(sample = avg_imbalance))+
  geom_qq() +
  geom_qq_line()

shapiro.test(prs_gait$avg_imbalance)
```

### Analysis of association

```{r}
# Spearman correlation between PRS and gait imbalance
# Spearman is used because PRS is not normally distributed
cor.test(
  prs_gait$PRS,
  prs_gait$avg_imbalance,
  method = "spearman"
)

# Fit linear regression within each treatment group
prs_fit_control  <- lm(prs_gait$avg_imbalance[treatment =="L-DOPA control"] ~ prs_gait$PRS[treatment == "L-DOPA control"], data = prs_gait)

prs_fit_new_compound  <- lm(prs_gait$avg_imbalance[treatment =="New compound"] ~ prs_gait$PRS[treatment == "New compound"], data = prs_gait)

summary(prs_fit_control)
summary(prs_fit_new_compound)

# Extract and perform Shapiro test on residuals of linear model in each treatment group:
shapiro.test(resid(prs_fit_control))
shapiro.test(resid(prs_fit_new_compound))



# Plot gait against PRS score and visualize linear regression within each group, with Pearson correlation:
prs_gait %>% 
  ggplot(aes(PRS, avg_imbalance, colour = treatment))+
  geom_point()+
  theme_classic()+
  geom_smooth(method = lm)+
  labs(y = "Gait")
  theme(text = element_text(family = "Helvetica", face = "bold"),
        axis.line = element_line(linewidth = 1.3),
        axis.ticks = element_line(linewidth = 1.3),
        axis.ticks.length = unit(0.1, "inch")
  )+
  stat_regline_equation(
    aes(label = after_stat(eq.label)),
    label.x = 0.5,
    label.y = c(17, 16)    
  ) +
  stat_cor(
    aes(label = after_stat(p.label)),
    label.x = 1.2,
    label.y = c(17, 16)  
  )+
  annotate("text", x = 0.9, y = 19, label = "Linear regression")


```

### Results: Gait vs PRS

The scatterplot showed a weak negative trend between PRS and mean absolute gait imbalance (see first scatterplot in previous section).

Normality was assessed using QQ plots and Shapiro-Wilk tests. PRS was not normally distributed (W = 0.808, p = 0.00348), while gait imbalance showed no significant departure from normality (W = 0.969, p = 0.8197). Therefore, Spearman's rank correlation was used to assess the relationship between the two datasets.

The analysis showed a weak negative correlation between PRS and gait imbalance (p = -0.232, p = 0.3852). However, this relationship was not statistically significant (p \> 0.05).

These results suggests that there is insufficient evidence of an association between polygenic risk and gait imbalance in the clinical trial patients. However, the small sample size (n = 16) limits the statistical power of this analysis. Other factors such as treatment, exercise and age, may also influence gait performance.

However the pattern is very different when patients are grouped by treatment. First I construct linear regression model within each group, then extract and run Shapiro test on residuals of each model to confirm normal distribution of residuals (both p\>0.05). From the linear model (constructed using lm() and visualized on the plot), association between PRS and balance in patient group receiving L-DOPA is not statistically significant (linear regression p = 0.08), but there is a strong negative association between PRS and balance in the new treatment group (slope = -2.8, p = 0.008). This indicates PRS score is a potential predictor of response to the new compound, which is interesting because Parkinson disease patients tend to have higher PRS score than healthy people.
